title: Venous hypertension caused by a meningioma involving the sigmoid sinus: case report
case_prompt: A 39-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of discomfort in both eyes. Fundoscopic examination revealed bilateral papilledema, and neuro-ophthalmologic testing showed mild visual field defects. She had no headaches, diplopia, focal weakness, or sensory disturbances, and her neurologic examination was otherwise normal. She was overweight (BMI 27.2 kg/m2), with an unremarkable medical and family history and no current medications. Lumbar puncture demonstrated an opening pressure of 500 mmH2O with normal cerebrospinal fluid composition. Noncontrast CT of the head showed no space-occupying lesions or hydrocephalus, only an incidental arachnoid cyst in the left middle fossa. MR imaging revealed a 2.5 cm lesion in the right sigmoid sinus that was isointense on T1- and T2-weighted images and showed homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. CT venography then demonstrated subtotal occlusion of the dominant right sigmoid sinus caused by a well-defined, homogeneous, hypodense mass.
diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Meningioma was considered as the most common neoplasm causing venous hypertension — “Meningiomas are the most common neoplastic lesion causing venous hypertension.” 2. Other tumors (eg, solitary fibrous tumor/hemangiopericytoma, osteoma, osteoblastoma, epidermoid cyst, metastatic carcinoma, Ewing sarcoma, cholesteatoma) were considered as potential causes of sinus obstruction — “Intracranial tumor compressing or invading the dural sinuses including meningioma…, solitary fibrous tumor/hemangiopericytoma, osteoma, osteoblastoma, epidermoid cyst, metastatic carcinoma…, Ewing sarcoma, and cholesteatoma must be distinguished from venous thrombosis or IIH.”
